name: Rayleigh–Taylor, Single Mode
question: Can the early growth of one interface mode be measured consistently?
blurb: A single small-amplitude cosine ripple with two wavelengths across the box. One bubble and one spike per wavelength grow before the nonlinear mushroom stage.
physics:
Put a dense fluid on top of a lighter one in gravity and the configuration stores potential energy it 'wants' to release by overturning. It is unstable to the smallest perturbation: a tiny dip in the interface lets heavy fluid poke down into light fluid, where it is even less supported, so the dip grows. Heavy fluid falls in narrow spikes; light fluid rises in broad bubbles.

As a spike accelerates through the lighter fluid it shears against it, and that shear is itself Kelvin–Helmholtz unstable — so the tip of each spike curls over into the iconic mushroom cap, and the caps in turn shed smaller vortices. The flow thus couples a large-scale buoyant overturning to a cascade of smaller shear instabilities, which is why it mixes so efficiently.

The Rayleigh–Taylor instability is everywhere there is acceleration across a density jump: the expanding remnants of supernovae, the compression of fuel in inertial-confinement fusion, rising salt domes in geology, and overturning in the oceans and atmosphere.
terms:
• u, ∂t u + (u·∇)u, −∇p, ν∇²u, ∇·u=0 — the incompressible Navier–Stokes terms
• −g·ρ·ŷ — the gravitational body force; heavier fluid (larger ρ) is pulled down harder, which is the source of the instability
• ρ here is an advected density field carried with the flow
• A = (ρ_heavy − ρ_light)/(ρ_heavy + ρ_light) — the Atwood number sets the density contrast across the interface; the spike growth rate scales like √(A·g·k), so higher A gives faster, narrower fingers
numerics: The same constant-density projection solver with an advected scalar ρ that enters only the gravitational body force (a Boussinesq-like approximation: inertia does not change with density). The interface is seeded with a multi-mode ripple, or a single mode of chosen wavenumber.
ic: Heavy fluid resting on light fluid, separated by a small multi-mode interface ripple; everything at rest.
bc: Closed, no-penetration top and bottom; free-slip side walls — a sealed box.
validation: Numerical check (consistency across resolutions); the linear growth rate is not compared with theory because the model is Boussinesq-like and viscous.

experiment.name: Rayleigh–Taylor instability
experiment.question: How does the density contrast set the growth of the instability?

params.name: atwood
params.label: Atwood number
params.help: A = (ρ_heavy − ρ_light)/(ρ_heavy + ρ_light), the density contrast across the interface. Higher A → faster, narrower spikes. (Boussinesq-like model: density only enters the buoyancy force; see the scene notes.)

params.name: gravity
params.label: Gravity
params.help: Gravity driving the instability. Higher → faster fingering / collapse.

params.name: viscosity
params.label: Viscosity
params.help: Kinematic viscosity ν — how 'thick' the fluid is. Lower → finer, more chaotic structures; higher → smoother, damped flow.

params.name: perturbation
params.label: Interface ripple
params.help: Amplitude of the initial interface ripple that seeds the fingers.

params.name: modes
params.label: Single-mode wavenumber
params.help: 0 = the multi-mode ripple (modes 3 + 7). A value n ≥ 1 seeds a single cosine mode with n wavelengths across the box and a small amplitude, for measuring the early growth of one mode.

params.name: resolution
params.label: Resolution
params.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

params.name: duration
params.label: Duration (×)
params.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
